title: Triangular coordinates and polynomial basis for the projective order algebra
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $r\ge0$, and $B=k[X_0,\ldots,X_r]$ with the grading by total degree [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-pc-standard-graded-algebra]. Let $\mathfrak p\subset k[t_1,\ldots,t_r]$ be a prime ideal, $L=k[t_1,\ldots,t_r]_{\mathfrak p}$, and $N=\mathfrak pL$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. Write $\delta(f)=f(1,t_1,\ldots,t_r)/1$, $U_d=\{f\in B_d:\delta(f)\in N^d\}$, and $U=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}U_d$. For any ideal $J$, write $\operatorname{ord}_J(h)=\sup\{n:h\in J^n\}$, with value $\infty$ for membership in every power. After a permutation of $X_1,\ldots,X_r$ (and the corresponding $t_i$), fixing $X_0$, there exist $0\le e\le r$, integers $1\le q_1\le\cdots\le q_e$, and $c_{i\ell}\in k$ such that, with the convention $X_{r+1}=X_0$,
$$\sigma_i=X_i^{q_i}+\sum_{\ell=i+1}^{r+1}c_{i\ell}X_\ell^{q_i}\quad(1\le i\le e),\qquad U=k[\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_e].$$
In characteristic zero every $q_i=1$; in positive characteristic every $q_i$ is a power of the characteristic. The elements $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_e,X_{e+1},\ldots,X_r,X_0$ are algebraically independent. Put $\Delta=\{\beta\in\mathbf N^e:0\le\beta_i<q_i\}$ and $q\cdot A=\sum_iq_iA_i$. Every $f\in B_d$ has a unique finite expansion
$$f=\sum_{A\in\mathbf N^e,\,\beta\in\Delta}f_{A\beta}(X_{e+1},\ldots,X_r,X_0)\sigma^AX_1^{\beta_1}\cdots X_e^{\beta_e},$$
where $f_{A\beta}$ is homogeneous of degree $d-q\cdot A-|\beta|$ and is zero if that number is negative. Empty tuples and $e=0$ are included.

source.place: External source read online: Hironaka, Certain numerical characters of singularities, J. Math. Kyoto Univ. 10-1 (1970), section 13, (13.2), p.168; polynomial normal expansion at the start of Lemma 18, p.174. https://scispace.com/pdf/certain-numerical-characters-of-singularities-18d51ii5bz.pdf. Archival copy WANTED; the ILO document is the VIII 2.3.13 ancestor motivation only. No Stacks tag states this specialized assertion.

proof.text: Write $A=k[t_1,\ldots,t_r]$ and introduce an invertible indeterminate $u$. The substitutions $X_0\mapsto u$, $X_i\mapsto t_i u$, with inverse $t_i\mapsto X_i/X_0$, identify $B[X_0^{-1}]$ with $A[u,u^{-1}]$ by the polynomial universal property. Let $\mathfrak q\subset B$ be the inverse image of $\mathfrak pA[u,u^{-1}]$. Its quotient embeds in the Laurent polynomial ring over the domain $A/\mathfrak p$, so $\mathfrak q$ is prime. It is homogeneous: for $h=\sum_dh_d$, its image is $\sum_du^d h_d(1,t)$, and membership in $\mathfrak pA[u,u^{-1}]$ is coefficientwise. Also $X_0\notin\mathfrak q$. The fraction description of localization then identifies $B_{\mathfrak q}$ with $C=(L[u,u^{-1}])_{N L[u,u^{-1}]}$: all denominators on either side are precisely those with nonzero image in the fraction field of $(A/\mathfrak p)[u,u^{-1}]$.

source.place: Agent argument compared with online Hironaka (1970), section 13, (13.2), printed p.168, and Lemma 18, p.174; online Dietel (2014), Remark 1.4.3 and Lemma 1.4.4, printed pp.17–18. Archival copies WANTED; ILO VIII 2.3.13 is ancestor motivation only.

proof.text: For $g\in L$ and $d\ge0$ one has $g\in N^dC$ if and only if $g\in N^d$. The reverse implication is extension of an ideal. For the forward implication, the fraction definition supplies a Laurent polynomial $s\notin N L[u,u^{-1}]$ with $sg\in N^d L[u,u^{-1}]$. Some coefficient $s_j$ lies outside $N$ and is a unit of the local ring $L$; coefficientwise membership gives $s_jg\in N^d$, hence $g\in N^d$. For $f\in B_d$ its image in $C$ is $u^d\delta(f)$, and $u$ is a unit. Thus $f/1\in(\mathfrak qB_{\mathfrak q})^d$ if and only if $\delta(f)\in N^d$. This checks the equality of our degree pieces with those in [lem-trf-projective-order-algebra-additive-generators]. Its hypothesis that the homogeneous prime misses the irrelevant ideal holds because it misses $X_0$. Applying that node, $U$ is a graded $k$-subalgebra generated by all its positive-degree homogeneous additive elements.

source.place: Agent argument compared with online Hironaka (1970), section 13, (13.2), printed p.168, and Lemma 18, p.174; online Dietel (2014), Remark 1.4.3 and Lemma 1.4.4, printed pp.17–18. Archival copies WANTED; ILO VIII 2.3.13 is ancestor motivation only.

proof.text: For $d>0$ let $Q_d$ be the vector space of additive elements of $U_d$, including zero. The cited classification says every nonzero element is a linear combination of the pure $d$th powers of the variables; its degree is $1$ in characteristic zero and a power of $p$ in characteristic $p$. Sums and scalar multiples remain additive. In positive characteristic $h\in Q_d$ implies $h^{p^a}\in Q_{dp^a}$: the identity $(v+w)^p=v^p+w^p$ follows by the binomial expansion (the intermediate binomial coefficients are divisible by $p$), and $\delta(h^{p^a})\in (N^d)^{p^a}=N^{dp^a}$. Finally $Q_d\cap k[X_0]=0$, since a nonzero homogeneous polynomial there is $cX_0^d$, whose image $c$ is a unit of $L$, hence is outside $N^d$.

source.place: Agent argument compared with online Hironaka (1970), section 13, (13.2), printed p.168, and Lemma 18, p.174; online Dietel (2014), Remark 1.4.3 and Lemma 1.4.4, printed pp.17–18. Archival copies WANTED; ILO VIII 2.3.13 is ancestor motivation only.

proof.text: Here is the pivot construction, with $X_0$ always last and never permuted. At stage $i$ put $R_{i,d}=Q_d\cap k[X_i,\ldots,X_r,X_0]$, initially $i=1$. If all these spaces vanish, stop and put $e=i-1$. Otherwise choose the smallest positive degree $q_i$ with $R_{i,q_i}\ne0$ and take a nonzero element there. By step 3 it is a sum of pure $q_i$th powers. Some variable among $X_i,\ldots,X_r$ has a nonzero coefficient, since a pure $X_0$ form is impossible. Permute only these remaining variables to make it $X_i$ and divide by its coefficient. This gives $\sigma_i=X_i^{q_i}+\sum_{\ell=i+1}^{r+1}c_{i\ell}X_\ell^{q_i}$, with $X_{r+1}=X_0$, inside $Q_{q_i}$. Define the next residual spaces using the variables after this pivot. They are subspaces of the preceding residual spaces, so each later chosen degree is at least the previous one. After at most $r$ pivots the residual spaces lie in $k[X_0]$ and vanish. Thus the construction terminates, yields $0\le e\le r$, and has the asserted characteristic restrictions on the $q_i$.

source.place: Agent argument compared with online Hironaka (1970), section 13, (13.2), printed p.168, and Lemma 18, p.174; online Dietel (2014), Remark 1.4.3 and Lemma 1.4.4, printed pp.17–18. Archival copies WANTED; ILO VIII 2.3.13 is ancestor motivation only.

proof.text: To verify that the construction exhausts all additive generators, fix $h\in R_{i,d}$. If $h\ne0$ then $d\ge q_i$. In characteristic $p$, both degrees are powers of $p$, so $d/q_i$ is a power of $p$; in characteristic zero both are $1$. Let $b$ be the coefficient of $X_i^d$ in $h$. The polynomial $h-b\sigma_i^{d/q_i}$ has no $X_i$ term and lies in $R_{i+1,d}$, by step 3 and the pure-power form in the classification. Consequently, inducting on the stage, each $h\in Q_d$ is a sum of scalar multiples of powers of $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_e$, plus an element of $R_{e+1,d}=0$. Each $\sigma_i$ is in $U$, and all the additive generators of $U$ lie in $k[\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_e]$. The additive-generation node therefore gives $U=k[\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_e]$. The induction also covers the initial stop $e=0$, where all $Q_d$ vanish and $U=k$.

source.place: Agent argument compared with online Hironaka (1970), section 13, (13.2), printed p.168, and Lemma 18, p.174; online Dietel (2014), Remark 1.4.3 and Lemma 1.4.4, printed pp.17–18. Archival copies WANTED; ILO VIII 2.3.13 is ancestor motivation only.

proof.text: Use the lexicographic order $X_1>\cdots>X_r>X_0$ on monomials. In the expansion of $\sigma_i$ the leading monomial is $X_i^{q_i}$ with coefficient $1$. Direct multiplication of finite polynomials shows that the leading exponent of $\sigma^A X_1^{\beta_1}\cdots X_e^{\beta_e}X_{e+1}^{\gamma_{e+1}}\cdots X_r^{\gamma_r}X_0^{\gamma_0}$ is $(q_1A_1+\beta_1,\ldots,q_eA_e+\beta_e,\gamma_{e+1},\ldots,\gamma_r,\gamma_0)$, again with coefficient $1$. If $0\le\beta_i<q_i$, these exponents are distinct for distinct triples $(A,\beta,\gamma)$, by uniqueness of quotient and remainder of an integer by $q_i$. In a nonzero finite scalar relation choose the largest of these leading exponents: no summand with a smaller leading exponent contains its monomial, so its coefficient cannot cancel. Hence these polynomials are linearly independent over $k$. Taking $\beta=0$ also shows that the $e+(r-e)+1$ elements $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_e,X_{e+1},\ldots,X_r,X_0$ have no nonzero polynomial relation, which is algebraic independence.

source.place: Agent argument compared with online Hironaka (1970), section 13, (13.2), printed p.168, and Lemma 18, p.174; online Dietel (2014), Remark 1.4.3 and Lemma 1.4.4, printed pp.17–18. Archival copies WANTED; ILO VIII 2.3.13 is ancestor motivation only.

proof.text: For existence of the expansion, first take a monomial of degree $d$. Whenever the exponent of some $X_i$, $1\le i\le e$, is at least $q_i$, replace one factor $X_i^{q_i}$ by $\sigma_i-\sum_{\ell>i}c_{i\ell}X_\ell^{q_i}$. Treat the $\sigma$ factors as coefficients during this reduction. In every resulting term the exponent tuple of $(X_1,\ldots,X_e)$ decreases strictly in lexicographic order. The total weighted degree, assigning degree $q_i$ to $\sigma_i$ and degree $1$ to every $X_j$, stays $d$. There are only finitely many such tuples of degree at most $d$, so each branch of this finite reduction terminates. It produces a finite sum with all $\beta_i<q_i$. Extend by linearity to $f\in B_d$ and group terms by $(A,\beta)$; the remaining polynomials use only $X_{e+1},\ldots,X_r,X_0$. Each of their monomials has degree $d-q\cdot A-|\beta|$, giving the required homogeneity and vanishing for negative degree. Uniqueness follows from the scalar linear independence proved in step 6 after expanding each coefficient polynomial. For $e=0$ this is the original polynomial expression in all variables, and the same argument includes $r=0$ and $d=0$.
